text: Chapter four. Cowries: the money that got too heavy to carry.
For centuries, much of West Africa used a small seashell as money: the cowrie. Most came from the Maldives, in the Indian Ocean.
One shell bought very little, so people counted them. Forty to a string. Two thousand to a head.
West African traders wanted shells: their markets ran on them. So European ships brought shells by the ton, to buy enslaved people... and later, palm oil.
In eighteen forty-five, a Hamburg firm found a shortcut. In Zanzibar, local traders sold a bigger cowrie for far less. The firm shipped some to Dahomey.
German and French firms followed. Coastal merchants bought them: they were cheap. By one estimate, sixteen billion shells poured in.

In Dahomey, a silver dollar cost about two thousand shells in the eighteen forties. By the eighteen eighties: twenty thousand. A family that had saved two thousand shells now held a tenth of a dollar. They hadn't spent a single one.
And the money got heavy. Around nineteen hundred in Lagos, one small silver shilling was worth four thousand shells. A coin in your fist... or a sack on your head.
Remember Ulm Hollow's bogwool? Too bulky to be money. Flood a money, and it turns into bogwool. Wren found a cave. Hamburg found a reef. Next: what if Wren... is the emperor?
